title: Undo and Redo
subtitle: {key:u} to undo. {key:Ctrl-R} to redo. Experiment without fear.
summary: {key:u} undoes the last change. {key:Ctrl-R} redoes it. Repeat either command to walk through multiple changes, and experiment without fear.

blocks.text: Undo is your permission to experiment. Try the unfamiliar motion. Run the command whose effect you cannot predict. If it changes the wrong text, press {key:u}. If you decide that the change was right after all, press {key:Ctrl-R}. You do not need to understand every command before trying it.

Press {key:u} repeatedly to walk backward through multiple changes. Press {key:Ctrl-R} repeatedly to walk forward again. Counts work too: {key:5}{key:u} undoes the last five changes. Make a mess on purpose, undo it, and keep going. Fearlessness is a practical Vim skill.

What counts as "a change"? An entire Insert-mode session, from {key:i} to {key:Esc}, is one change. An operator+motion (like {key:d}{key:w}) is one change. A single {key:x} or {key:r} is one change. So {key:u} undoes the *last meaningful action*, not the last keystroke.

Vim stores undo history as a tree rather than throwing away an old redo path when you undo and then make a different change. You do not need the tree commands yet: {key:u} and {key:Ctrl-R} are enough for ordinary editing. [Undo as a Tree](#survival.undo-tree) later explains branches, chronological traversal, `:undolist`, `:earlier`, and persistent undo.
{key:U} (capital) is a less-common command: it undoes *all changes on the current line* since you last moved off it. Useful occasionally; the regular {key:u} is what you'll use 99% of the time.

rows: Undo all changes on the current line

blocks.title: Undo units are command-shaped, not keystroke-shaped
blocks.text: The undo system batches edits at command boundaries, not per keystroke. One normal-mode command — including a complete insert session from {key:i} through {key:Esc} — collapses into a single undo unit. That's why hitting {key:u} after typing a paragraph rips out the whole paragraph at once: the editor only inserted one undo boundary, at the moment you returned to *normal mode.* Internally undo is a tree of state snapshots; redo is a forward walk through that tree.
